 1. What Is Photogrammetry?
 Definition
 Photogrammetry is the science and engineering of obtaining reliable measurements, geometry, and spatial
 information about objects or environments from photographs. In modern practice it often means using many
 overlapping digital images, camera calibration, image matching, geometric reconstruction, georeferencing,
 and surface generation to create maps and 3D models.

 The central idea
 A single photograph records a 3D scene onto a 2D sensor, so depth is ambiguous. Multiple photographs taken
 from different viewpoints create parallax: the same physical feature appears at different image positions. If
 camera geometry is known or estimated, those observations constrain the 3D location of the feature.
 Repeating this for thousands or millions of features produces a sparse or dense representation of the scene.

 Why multiple images matter
 Photogrammetry is not simply stitching pictures together. Image overlap provides redundant geometric
 observations. Redundancy allows the software to estimate camera positions, recover 3D coordinates, detect
 inconsistent measurements, and improve results through optimization. Good overlap and good image texture
 are therefore fundamental.

 Main product families
 Typical outputs include oriented cameras, sparse tie-point clouds, dense point clouds, meshes, textured
 models, orthophotos or orthomosaics, DSMs, DTMs, contours, cross-sections, measurements, volumes, and
 GIS-ready raster/vector layers.

 Photogrammetry versus ordinary photography
 Photography emphasizes visual appearance. Photogrammetry emphasizes measurable geometry. A visually
 excellent set of images can still produce a poor survey if scale, camera calibration, overlap, control, exposure
 consistency, or geometry is inadequate.

 Common platforms
 Modern projects use UAVs, aircraft, satellites, handheld cameras, smartphones, tripod-mounted cameras,
 vehicle-mounted systems, and multi-camera rigs. The platform changes the acquisition geometry and
 operational constraints, but the underlying principles remain similar.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 2. Related Concepts and Vocabulary
 Important related topics
 To understand photogrammetry properly, also learn: perspective projection; interior and exterior orientation;
 camera calibration; epipolar geometry; parallax; feature extraction; image matching; tie points; scale ambiguity;
 coordinate frames; bundle adjustment; robust estimation; georeferencing; geodetic datums; GNSS; RTK/PPK;
 ground sampling distance; radiometric calibration; point-cloud classification; surface reconstruction; texture
 mapping; orthorectification; DSM/DTM; accuracy assessment; uncertainty propagation; and metadata.

 Active versus passive sensing
 Photogrammetry is primarily a passive optical technique: it observes reflected light rather than emitting its own
 ranging signal. LiDAR is an active ranging technique. The two can be complementary. Photogrammetry can
 provide dense color-rich geometry, while LiDAR can be stronger in low-texture surfaces or vegetation


Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                      Page 3
Page 4 of 42 
 penetration scenarios depending on the system.

 A useful mental model
 Think of a photogrammetric project as a chain: acquisition -> image quality -> image alignment ->
 camera/network estimation -> georeferencing -> dense reconstruction -> surface/model generation -> map
 production -> validation. Errors introduced early propagate downstream.


 3. Image Formation and Camera Geometry
 Perspective projection
 A simplified pinhole camera maps a 3D point onto an image plane according to perspective projection. In
 normalized coordinates, image coordinates are approximately proportional to X/Z and Y/Z, where Z is depth
 along the camera axis. This is why distant objects appear smaller.

 Interior orientation
 Interior orientation describes the camera’s internal geometry: focal length or principal distance, principal point,
 and lens distortion parameters. Modern software often estimates these parameters during calibration or
 bundle adjustment rather than relying only on a laboratory calibration.

 Exterior orientation
 Exterior orientation describes the camera’s position and orientation in the world. Six parameters are commonly
 used: three translations and three rotations. In UAV projects, GNSS/IMU observations can provide useful initial
 estimates.

 Lens distortion
 Real lenses depart from the ideal pinhole model. Radial distortion can bend straight lines, while tangential or
 decentering distortion arises from lens alignment. Strong distortion near image edges can affect
 reconstruction if it is not modeled adequately.

 Field of view and focal length
 Longer focal lengths generally narrow the field of view and increase image scale for a given distance; shorter
 focal lengths widen the field of view. Focal length interacts with altitude, sensor size, and desired GSD, so it
 cannot be evaluated in isolation.

 Ground Sampling Distance
 GSD is the approximate ground dimension represented by one image pixel. A simplified relationship is GSD H
 * p / f, where H is camera-to-ground distance, p is pixel pitch, and f is focal length. Real-world GSD also depends
 on terrain relief, camera attitude, lens geometry, and processing assumptions.


 4. Structure-from-Motion (SfM)
 What SfM does
 Structure-from-Motion estimates camera motion and scene structure from overlapping images without
 requiring the camera trajectory to be known in advance. It is a major reason modern photogrammetry became
 accessible for UAV, terrestrial, and close-range applications.

 Typical SfM sequence
 The software detects distinctive image features, matches them across overlapping photographs, rejects
 implausible correspondences, estimates relative camera poses, triangulates initial 3D points, and jointly refines
 camera parameters and 3D point coordinates.



Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                  Page 4
Page 5 of 42 
 Scale ambiguity
 Purely image-based reconstruction can determine geometry up to an arbitrary scale and coordinate frame.
 Ground control, measured distances, known camera positions, or other constraints are needed to establish
 physical scale and geospatial reference.

 Network geometry
 A strong image network has sufficient overlap and varied viewing geometry. If every image is nearly identical in
 position and orientation, depth can become weakly constrained. Oblique imagery and cross-strips can improve
 geometry in suitable projects.

 SfM limitations
 Homogeneous surfaces, repetitive patterns, moving objects, reflections, transparent materials, severe
 shadows, extreme exposure differences, vegetation motion, and inadequate overlap can reduce reliable
 matching.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 5. Feature Detection, Matching, and Tie Points
 Features
 Features are visually distinctive image structures such as corners, textured patches, or local intensity patterns.
 Modern algorithms identify features that can be recognized across different viewpoints and scales.

 Tie points
 A tie point represents a matched visual feature observed in multiple images. A large and well-distributed
 tie-point network is generally more useful than a huge number of poorly distributed matches.

 Matching quality
 Matching should be evaluated spatially, not only by count. If thousands of matches cluster in one textured area
 while large regions have none, the camera network may still be weak.

 Outlier rejection
 Some matches are wrong. Robust estimation methods identify and suppress correspondences inconsistent
 with a coherent camera and scene geometry. Outlier rejection is essential because a small number of bad
 matches can distort camera estimation.

 Image overlap
 Forward overlap and side overlap are planning variables. High overlap improves redundancy and matching
 opportunities, but it also increases the number of images and processing load. The right values depend on
 terrain, speed, camera, altitude, lighting, and project accuracy requirements.


 6. Triangulation and Camera Pose
 Triangulation
 Triangulation estimates a 3D point from observations of that point in two or more images whose camera
 geometry is known or estimated. Conceptually, each image observation defines a ray from the camera through
 the image point. The 3D location is where the rays intersect, or where they come closest in a noisy system.

 Parallax

Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                      Page 5
Page 6 of 42 
 Parallax is the apparent displacement of a feature between viewpoints. Greater baseline generally creates
 stronger depth information, but excessive baseline can make matching harder. Photogrammetric design is
 therefore a balance between geometric strength and correspondence reliability.

 Epipolar geometry
 For two views, the projection of one camera center into the other image defines an epipole, and a point in one
 image corresponds to an epipolar line in the other. This relationship reduces the search space for matching and
 is foundational to stereo reconstruction.

 Camera pose
 Pose is the position and orientation of a camera relative to a coordinate system. Accurate pose estimates are
 central to reliable triangulation. GNSS/IMU observations can provide priors, while image measurements refine
 them.

 Ray intersection in practice
 Because measurements contain noise, rays usually do not intersect perfectly. Algorithms minimize geometric
 or reprojection error, sometimes using weighted observations and robust loss functions.


 7. Bundle Adjustment and Self-Calibration
 Bundle adjustment
 Bundle adjustment jointly optimizes camera parameters and 3D point coordinates so that the projected 3D
 points best agree with their measured image observations. It is one of the most important optimization steps in
 modern photogrammetry.

 Reprojection error
 If a reconstructed 3D point is projected into an image, the difference between predicted and observed pixel
 position is the reprojection error. Low average error is useful, but it does not by itself prove survey accuracy; a
 model can be internally consistent yet incorrectly georeferenced.

 Self-calibration
 Self-calibration estimates camera interior orientation parameters from the image network. It can compensate
 for changes in focus, zoom, temperature, or other effects, but only when the network geometry sufficiently
 constrains those parameters.

 Gauge freedoms
 Without external constraints, a reconstruction may have arbitrary translation, rotation, and scale. Fixing or
 constraining reference observations removes these degrees of freedom.

 Practical interpretation
 Bundle adjustment is the mathematical engine that turns many noisy observations into a coherent
 camera-and-scene solution. Understanding it helps explain why good control, image geometry, and accurate
 observations matter.


 8. Point Clouds
 What is a point cloud?
 A point cloud is a collection of 3D points representing a surface or volume. Points may include XYZ coordinates,
 color, intensity, classification, normal vectors, confidence, or other attributes.

 Sparse versus dense

Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                   Page 6
Page 7 of 42 
 Sparse point clouds contain mainly tie points used for camera/network reconstruction. Dense point clouds
 attempt to reconstruct much more of the visible surface and are used for mapping, measurement, modeling,
 and surface generation.

 Dense matching
 Multi-view stereo estimates dense depth by finding correspondences across multiple images after camera
 geometry has been solved. The result can contain millions or billions of points for large projects.

 Point density
 High point density is not synonymous with high accuracy. Duplicating or oversampling uncertain information
 does not create true geometric precision. Point spacing should be interpreted alongside GSD, image quality,
 viewing geometry, and independent checkpoints.

 Cleaning and classification
 Point clouds may need noise filtering, ground classification, vegetation/building separation, decimation, and
 region-of-interest extraction. Classification should be validated because automated labels can fail in complex
 terrain.

 Common formats
 LAS/LAZ, PLY, XYZ, and application-specific formats are widely used. Selection depends on downstream GIS,
 CAD, BIM, visualization, and storage requirements.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 9. 3D Meshes and Surface Reconstruction
 Mesh definition
 A 3D mesh represents a surface using vertices, edges, and faces, commonly triangles. It converts a point-based
 representation into connected surface geometry.

 Why meshes are useful
 Meshes support visualization, volume computation, inspection, texture mapping, simulation, reverse
 engineering, cultural heritage documentation, and asset management.

 Surface reconstruction
 Algorithms infer a continuous surface from points. Common strategies differ in how they handle holes, noise,
 sharp edges, density variation, and watertightness.

 Texture mapping
 A textured mesh uses photographs to assign color or imagery to the surface. Good texture requires consistent
 camera imagery, sufficient overlap, and correct surface geometry.

 Mesh pitfalls
 A dense mesh can faithfully reproduce noise, vegetation, moving objects, or artifacts. Over-smoothing can
 erase real detail. Mesh quality should therefore be judged against the intended use, not merely triangle count.


 10. Orthophotos and Orthomosaics
 Orthophoto


Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                      Page 7
Page 8 of 42 
 An orthophoto is an image corrected for perspective and terrain/surface relief so that scale is more uniform
 and the image can be used as a map layer. An orthomosaic combines multiple orthorectified images into a
 continuous mosaic.

 Why raw images are not maps
 A raw photograph contains perspective displacement. Buildings lean, terrain relief shifts features, and scale
 changes across the image. Orthorectification uses camera geometry and a surface model to compensate for
 these effects.

 Seamlines
 An orthomosaic must choose which image contributes each area. Seamline selection can be affected by image
 quality, view angle, shadows, moving objects, and surface discontinuities.

 Radiometric consistency
 Differences in exposure, white balance, vignetting, and illumination can produce visible seams. Good
 acquisition conditions and radiometric correction reduce these problems.

 Map use
 Orthomosaics are useful for inspection, digitization, land-use mapping, construction documentation,
 agriculture, disaster assessment, and GIS basemaps. Their accuracy must still be validated with independent
 control.


 11. DEM, DSM, DTM, and Terrain Products
 DSM
 A Digital Surface Model represents the elevation of visible surfaces, which may include roofs, trees, vehicles,
 and the ground.

 DTM
 A Digital Terrain Model is intended to represent bare-earth terrain. It normally requires filtering or classification
 to remove above-ground objects.

 DEM
 DEM is often used as a generic term for digital elevation data and can refer to a surface or terrain model
 depending on context. Always define what your project means by DEM.

 Generation workflow
 A common sequence is dense cloud -> classify ground -> interpolate ground points -> create terrain raster ->
 derive contours, slope, aspect, hillshade, profiles, or volumes.

 Interpolation
 Grid resolution should be appropriate to point density and terrain complexity. Very fine grids do not
 automatically contain more valid information; they may simply interpolate between points.

 Breaklines
 In engineered terrain, breaklines can preserve sharp features such as road edges, drainage channels, curbs,
 and retaining walls. Automated terrain generation may otherwise smooth or cross important discontinuities.


 12. Ground Control Points (GCPs) and Check Points

Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                    Page 8
Page 9 of 42 
 GCP definition
 A Ground Control Point is a clearly identifiable ground location whose coordinates are independently measured
 in the project coordinate system. GCPs constrain the photogrammetric solution and help establish scale,
 orientation, translation, and geospatial accuracy.

 Check points
 Check points are independent observations used to evaluate accuracy. They should not be used as control if the
 goal is an independent accuracy assessment.

 Distribution
 Control should cover the project area rather than clustering in one location. Edge and corner coverage is
 important because extrapolation outside the control network can reveal systematic distortion.

 Visibility
 A GCP must be clearly visible in enough images. A precise GNSS coordinate is useless if the image
 measurement is ambiguous.

 Accuracy hierarchy
 Control should normally be more accurate than the desired final product. Otherwise, control uncertainty can
 dominate the error budget.

 Target design
 Targets should have sufficient size and contrast for the planned GSD and flight height. Natural points can work,
 but artificial targets are often easier to identify and measure consistently.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 13. RTK and PPK Georeferencing
 RTK
 Real-Time Kinematic GNSS can provide high-precision positioning during data acquisition by using correction
 information. In UAV photogrammetry, the camera event position can be recorded with high precision when the
 system is properly configured.

 PPK
 Post-Processed Kinematic GNSS computes precise positions after the mission using recorded observations and
 reference information. It is useful when real-time correction links are unreliable or unavailable.

 RTK/PPK is not magic
 High-precision camera coordinates do not guarantee a high-accuracy map. Errors can remain in camera timing,
 lever-arm calibration, boresight, image synchronization, lens modeling, terrain, and surface reconstruction.

 Direct versus indirect georeferencing
 Direct georeferencing uses measured camera positions/orientations to constrain the model. Indirect
 georeferencing uses GCPs or other surveyed references. Many professional workflows use RTK/PPK together
 with a smaller number of checkpoints or GCPs for validation and robustness.

 Base and correction considerations



Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                      Page 9
Page 10 of 42 
 Reference stations, correction streams, coordinate frames, antenna heights, event timing, and datum
 transformations must be handled consistently. A technically precise GNSS observation can still be wrong if the
 reference frame is misunderstood.


 14. UAV / Drone Flight Planning
 Mission objective first
 Do not start by choosing altitude. Start with required accuracy, GSD, area, terrain, deliverables, and sensor
 constraints. Then select altitude, speed, overlap, camera settings, and control strategy.

 Altitude
 Altitude affects GSD, footprint, relief displacement, and coverage. Terrain-following missions can maintain
 more consistent GSD over variable terrain but require reliable elevation information and operational planning.

 Overlap
 Forward and side overlap create redundancy. Higher overlap is often helpful for difficult surfaces, but increases
 image count and processing time. The optimal values depend on application and camera.

 Flight speed and shutter
 If the shutter speed is too slow relative to flight speed, motion blur can reduce matching quality. The camera
 should generally use sufficiently fast shutter settings and appropriate ISO/aperture for the lighting conditions.

 Sun and shadows
 Consistent lighting is valuable for matching and orthomosaic quality. Harsh shadows can create texture
 changes that complicate matching. Reflective surfaces and low sun angles can be especially problematic.

 Terrain and obstacles
 Relief, buildings, trees, towers, power lines, and other obstacles affect safe altitude and image geometry.
 Regulatory requirements and site-specific hazards must be considered before flight.


 15. Image Acquisition and Field Practice
 Camera settings
 For mapping, fixed focus, stable exposure, sufficient shutter speed, and consistent image settings are
 commonly preferred. Automatic exposure can introduce large radiometric differences across a block.

 Focus
 Focus should be set deliberately. Refocusing during a mission can alter internal camera geometry and degrade
 consistency, especially on consumer cameras.

 Image quality
 Blur, underexposure, overexposure, compression artifacts, sensor noise, and lens contamination can reduce
 feature matching. More images do not compensate for systematically poor image quality.

 Ground photos
 Document GCPs, control monuments, environmental conditions, mission boundaries, equipment configuration,
 and unusual site conditions. Field notes can save hours during processing and QA.

 Data integrity


Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                   Page 10
Page 11 of 42 
 Keep original image files and GNSS logs unchanged. Use a clear naming convention and maintain backups.
 Record coordinate system, camera, lens, flight date, mission settings, and processing software/version.


 16. Agisoft Metashape Workflow
 Overview
 Agisoft Metashape is a commercial photogrammetry package widely used for image alignment, camera
 optimization, dense reconstruction, mesh generation, orthomosaic creation, elevation products,
 measurements, and geospatial export.

 Project setup
 Create a project and import the images. Inspect image metadata and verify that the intended camera/lens
 information is present. If using RTK/PPK positions, import or verify camera reference coordinates and
 coordinate system settings.

 Align Photos
 The alignment stage detects features, matches images, estimates camera poses, and creates a sparse point
 cloud. Review aligned camera coverage and tie-point distribution. Unaligned images are a warning sign, not
 something to ignore.

 Optimize Cameras
 After adding GCPs or verifying camera references, optimize camera calibration and orientation as appropriate.
 Review reprojection errors and residuals rather than relying on a single overall statistic.

 Build Depth Maps / Dense Cloud
 Use appropriate quality settings for the project. Higher quality increases processing time and memory use.
 Inspect the dense cloud for holes, noise, duplicated surfaces, and vegetation artifacts.

 Build Mesh
 Choose a surface source and reconstruction settings based on the intended deliverable. For terrain, a mesh
 from an unsuitable surface can produce misleading geometry.

 Build DEM
 Generate a digital elevation product from the appropriate source. If the goal is bare-earth terrain, classify
 ground points or use a terrain workflow rather than treating the raw surface as a DTM.

 Build Orthomosaic
 Select the appropriate surface and blending/seamline strategy. Inspect edges, buildings, vegetation, water, and
 moving objects for artifacts.

 Export
 Export products with a clearly documented CRS, resolution, vertical reference, units, and file format. Do not
 assume that a file coordinates are self-explanatory.

 Automation
 Metashape supports batch processing and scripting for repeatable workflows. Automation is valuable, but a
 script can reproduce mistakes at scale. Validate a representative project before automating a production
 pipeline.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.

 17. Accuracy, Error Sources, and QA/QC
 Accuracy versus precision
 Precision describes repeatability; accuracy describes closeness to the true or accepted value. A model can be
 internally precise but externally inaccurate if the georeferencing is wrong.

 Relative versus absolute accuracy
 Relative accuracy concerns geometry within the model. Absolute accuracy concerns alignment to an external
 coordinate system. GCPs, RTK/PPK, and independent checkpoints primarily address absolute accuracy.

 Major error sources
 Common errors include poor overlap, motion blur, weak texture, incorrect camera model, rolling-shutter
 effects, inaccurate GNSS event timing, wrong CRS, bad GCP coordinates, poor target identification,
 relief-related geometry weaknesses, moving vegetation, water, reflections, and processing parameter choices.

 RMSE
 Root Mean Square Error summarizes differences between estimated and reference coordinates. For n
 observations, RMSE is sqrt(mean(error^2)). Report horizontal and vertical components separately when
 appropriate. RMSE is useful but should not be treated as a complete description of error distribution.

 Residual inspection
 Inspect residuals spatially. A pattern where all checkpoints drift in one direction can indicate a systematic issue
 even if the average statistic appears acceptable.

 QA/QC checklist
 Verify image coverage; alignment; camera calibration; GCP residuals; independent checkpoint residuals;
 point-cloud artifacts; surface model artifacts; orthomosaic seams; CRS and units; metadata; and deliverable
 completeness.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 18. Coordinate Reference Systems and Geodesy
 CRS basics
 A coordinate reference system defines how coordinates relate to Earth. It may be geographic
 (latitude/longitude) or projected (easting/northing), with a datum and often a vertical reference.

 Horizontal versus vertical reference
 Horizontal coordinates and elevations can use different datums. A project can have correct horizontal
 coordinates but incorrect heights if the vertical reference is misunderstood.

 Ellipsoidal versus orthometric height
 GNSS commonly measures height relative to an ellipsoid, while engineering and mapping often require
 orthometric height related to a geoid model. The distinction matters.

 Units and transformations
 Meters versus feet, degrees versus projected units, and datum transformations can create large errors if
 mishandled. Always verify with known control points and project documentation.




Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                  Page 12
Page 13 of 42 
 Metadata discipline
 Every exported product should state CRS, units, resolution, vertical datum where applicable, source imagery,
 processing date/software, and accuracy information when available.


 19. Ground, Building, Vegetation, and Corridor Projects
 Open terrain
 Open, textured terrain is generally favorable. Large homogeneous fields, sand, snow, or water can be difficult
 because the images contain few stable features.

 Buildings
 Buildings benefit from oblique imagery because vertical walls are poorly represented by nadir-only images.
 Roof-only mapping can be adequate for some tasks but is insufficient for full 3D facades.

 Vegetation
 Vegetation is dynamic and changes shape with wind. Dense vegetation can produce a surface representing
 canopy rather than ground. Ground reconstruction beneath vegetation is often much harder than mapping the
 canopy.

 Corridors
 Roads, railways, canals, pipelines, and power corridors are elongated. Flight planning should provide adequate
 coverage along and across the corridor, with cross-strips or oblique imagery where needed to strengthen
 geometry.

 Stockpiles and volumes
 Photogrammetry can estimate stockpile volumes effectively when the base surface is known or reasonably
 modeled. The dominant uncertainty is often not the surface point density but the definition of the base and
 edges.


 20. Advanced Topics: Oblique, Thermal, Multispectral,
 and LiDAR Integration
 Oblique photogrammetry
 Oblique images view surfaces from angled perspectives. They improve facade coverage and can strengthen 3D
 geometry around structures, but introduce more complex occlusion and illumination conditions.

 Thermal
 Thermal cameras record long-wave infrared radiation rather than visible RGB. Their lower texture and different
 radiometry can make photogrammetric reconstruction harder. Thermal mapping often benefits from careful
 sensor calibration and sometimes a visible-light geometry solution used to support thermal products.

 Multispectral
 Multispectral cameras capture selected wavelength bands. They are valuable for vegetation and environmental
 analysis. Geometric alignment between bands and radiometric calibration are critical.

 LiDAR integration
 Combining LiDAR and photogrammetry can improve completeness and robustness. LiDAR can provide strong
 geometry where image texture is weak, while imagery adds color and detailed visual context.




Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                              Page 13
Page 14 of 42 
 Control integration
 Advanced projects may combine GCPs, RTK/PPK camera positions, total station observations, known distances,
 and external laser scans. The principle is to combine independent observations with appropriate uncertainty
 weighting.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 21. Troubleshooting and Failure Modes
 Images do not align
 Likely causes include insufficient overlap, blur, low texture, repetitive patterns, major exposure differences,
 wrong image metadata, or an acquisition pattern with weak geometry. First inspect the images and camera
 distribution rather than blindly changing software settings.

 Warped model
 Common causes include weak control, poor image geometry, rolling shutter, inaccurate camera positions,
 self-calibration instability, or insufficient cross-strip/oblique imagery. Adding more images from the same weak
 geometry may not solve the problem.

 Doming
 A bowl- or dome-shaped distortion can arise from weak network geometry and camera calibration correlations,
 particularly in certain nadir blocks. Stronger geometry and well-distributed control can help diagnose and
 constrain it.

 Noisy dense cloud
 Causes include poor image quality, water, vegetation motion, low texture, aggressive reconstruction settings,
 or incorrect depth-map assumptions. Filtering should not be used to hide systematic reconstruction failure.

 Orthomosaic seams
 Check exposure consistency, camera calibration, surface model quality, seamline selection, moving objects, and
 relief displacement. A good seamline cannot compensate for a bad surface model.

 Wrong coordinates
 Check CRS, datum, units, coordinate order, imported control, GNSS reference frame, geoid/vertical datum, and
 transformation settings. Coordinate problems are often metadata problems, not photogrammetry problems.


 22. Deliverables, Metadata, and Reporting
 Typical deliverable package
 Depending on the project: original images, aligned project, sparse cloud, dense cloud, mesh, textured model,
 orthomosaic, DSM, DTM, contours, checkpoints, accuracy report, control survey, flight log, metadata, and
 processing report.

 Report content
 A professional report should document purpose, site, acquisition date, platform, sensor, camera/lens, flight
 altitude, GSD, overlap, control strategy, CRS, processing software/version, major settings, quality checks,
 accuracy statistics, limitations, and final outputs.

 File naming

Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                  Page 14
Page 15 of 42 
 Use names that encode project, product, area, date/version, and resolution when useful. Avoid ambiguous
 names like final_final2.tif.

 Reproducibility
 Keep processing settings and software versions. A model that cannot be reproduced or audited is difficult to
 defend in engineering or regulatory contexts.


 23. Safety, Ethics, and Data Management
 Operational safety
 UAV operations require compliance with applicable aviation rules, site restrictions, privacy requirements, and
 manufacturer limits. Maintain situational awareness and do not prioritize data capture over safe operation.

 Privacy
 Images may capture people, homes, vehicles, or sensitive infrastructure. Data handling should respect
 applicable privacy and security obligations.

 Cyber and physical security
 Survey data can reveal site layouts, infrastructure, and assets. Use controlled storage, access permissions,
 backups, and secure transfer procedures where appropriate.

 Data retention
 Retain raw observations and key processing artifacts according to project requirements. Raw images are often
 the only way to reprocess a project when improved algorithms or corrections become available.


 24. Practical Project Workflows and Checklists
 End-to-end workflow
 1) define deliverables and accuracy; 2) choose sensor/platform; 3) design GSD and overlap; 4) establish CRS and
 control; 5) plan flight and safety; 6) acquire imagery; 7) verify data in the field; 8) align images; 9) inspect
 network; 10) add control/RTK/PPK; 11) optimize; 12) build dense cloud; 13) classify/filter; 14) generate
 mesh/DEM/DTM/orthomosaic; 15) validate checkpoints; 16) export; 17) document metadata and limitations.

 Field checklist
 Battery and storage capacity; camera/lens; focus; exposure; shutter; GNSS correction status; GCP targets; target
 coordinates; mission boundaries; obstacles; weather; wind; lighting; takeoff/landing zone; legal permissions;
 backup plan; field notes; post-flight image inspection.

 Processing checklist
 Confirm all images imported; inspect blur; confirm camera groups; inspect alignment; inspect tie-point
 distribution; verify CRS; verify control coordinates; optimize; inspect residuals; build dense cloud; inspect
 artifacts; create terrain/surface products; validate checkpoints; export with metadata.
 Practical note: The most common mistake is to optimize a downstream product before validating the upstream
 geometry. When a result looks wrong, move backward through the chain and find the first stage where the evidence
 becomes unreliable.



 25. Key Formulas and Technical Reference
 GSD approximation


Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                   Page 15
Page 16 of 42 
 GSD H*p/f, where H is camera-to-ground distance, p is pixel pitch, and f is focal length. This is a planning
 approximation, not a guarantee of final map accuracy.

 Scale intuition
 For a simplified vertical photograph, image scale is related to focal length divided by camera height above the
 reference surface. Terrain relief changes local scale and displacement.

 RMSE
 RMSE = sqrt((1/n) * sum(e_i^2)). For 2D horizontal error, use an appropriate horizontal error definition; for 3D
 error, define the metric explicitly.

 Triangulation intuition
 Each image observation defines a viewing ray. With two or more rays from known camera poses, solve for the
 3D point that best fits all observations.

 Reprojection error
 For observed image point x and projected model point x_hat, the residual is x - x_hat. Its magnitude in pixels is
 a common diagnostic.


 26. Glossary
 Bundle adjustment
 Joint optimization of camera parameters and 3D points to minimize image measurement residuals.

 Camera calibration
 Estimation of internal camera parameters and lens distortion.

 DEM
 Generic term for digital elevation model; project documentation should define whether it represents surface or
 terrain.

 DSM
 Digital Surface Model including visible objects such as buildings and vegetation.

 DTM
 Digital Terrain Model intended to represent bare-earth terrain.

 GCP
 Ground Control Point with independently surveyed coordinates used to constrain a model.

 GSD
 Ground Sampling Distance, approximate ground dimension corresponding to one pixel.

 Mesh
 Connected surface representation composed of vertices, edges, and faces.

 Orthomosaic
 Mosaic of orthorectified images assembled into a map-like image.




Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                  Page 16
Page 17 of 42 
 Parallax
 Apparent displacement caused by a change in viewpoint.

 PPK
 Post-Processed Kinematic GNSS positioning.

 RTK
 Real-Time Kinematic GNSS positioning using correction information.

 SfM
 Structure-from-Motion, image-based estimation of camera motion and scene structure.

 Tie point
 Matched image feature observed in multiple images and used in network reconstruction.

 Point cloud
 Set of 3D points representing scene geometry.

 Checkpoint
 Independent surveyed point used to assess accuracy rather than constrain the solution.

 Reprojection error
 Difference between observed and model-predicted image coordinates.

 Seamline
 Boundary selecting which source image contributes to an orthomosaic region.

 Control network
 Collection of surveyed observations constraining a photogrammetric model.

 Georeferencing
 Transforming or constraining model coordinates into a real-world coordinate system.


 27. Final Study Roadmap
 Begin with geometry
 Learn perspective projection, camera pose, parallax, triangulation, and epipolar geometry before memorizing
 software buttons. Software becomes much easier once the geometry is understood.

 Then learn the production chain
 Practice: images -> alignment -> sparse cloud -> control -> optimization -> dense cloud -> classification ->
 DEM/DTM -> orthomosaic -> QA/QC.

 Then learn accuracy
 Understand the difference between relative and absolute accuracy, GCPs and checkpoints, RMSE, systematic
 errors, CRS issues, and uncertainty.

 Then specialize


Photogrammetry - Comprehensive Technical Guide                                                                  Page 17
Page 18 of 42 
 Choose UAV mapping, terrestrial close-range photogrammetry, architecture/BIM, mining, agriculture,
 surveying, cultural heritage, inspection, corridor mapping, or scientific applications.

 Core principle
 A photogrammetric result is only as defensible as the acquisition design, geometric solution, georeferencing,
 independent validation, and documentation behind it. Treat the entire workflow as a measurement system, not
 as an image-processing trick.

    Product           Primary input               Best use                                Main caution

    Orthomosaic       Oriented images + surface   2D mapping, digitization, inspection    Relief, seams, moving objects

    DSM               Dense cloud                 Visible surface elevation               Vegetation/buildings included
