  1. Terrain & Elevation Models — The Conceptual Foundation
  Terrain and elevation modeling is the process of converting measured elevation observations into representations that can be
  analyzed, visualized, compared, and used to make decisions. The source observations may come from LiDAR,
  photogrammetry, GNSS surveying, total stations, radar, satellite products, bathymetry, or existing topographic datasets.

  The most important point is that a point cloud, a raster elevation model, a TIN, a contour map, and a terrain surface are not
  interchangeable objects. Each is a different representation with different assumptions and different strengths. A LiDAR point
  cloud is a collection of observations. A raster DEM samples elevation on a regular grid. A TIN represents a surface with
  irregularly connected triangles. Contours represent selected elevation levels as lines. A DTM may refer to a bare-earth
  surface or, depending on the specification, to a set of mass points and breaklines from which a surface is derived.

  The USGS emphasizes that DEM is used as a general term and that terminology varies between organizations and countries.
  In USGS usage, a generic DEM normally implies bare-earth terrain unless it is specifically identified as a DSM. A DTM can
  have a more specific vector meaning involving mass points and breaklines. Therefore, never assume the acronym alone tells
  you exactly what the dataset contains; inspect the metadata and specification.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  2. DEM — Digital Elevation Model
  A Digital Elevation Model is a digital representation of elevation. In common GIS practice it is frequently a raster containing
  elevation values at regularly spaced positions. USGS defines a DEM as a representation of bare ground in its general
  glossary and describes DEMs as regularly spaced elevation values referenced to a common vertical datum.

  A DEM is therefore not merely an image. Each cell contains a numerical elevation value. Displaying it with a grayscale or
  color ramp creates a visualization, but the underlying grid is quantitative.

  A DEM can be generated from LiDAR ground points, photogrammetric products, stereo imagery, radar, survey observations,
  contours, or other elevation sources. The source matters because the resulting accuracy, resolution, noise characteristics,
  void behavior, and vertical reference can differ dramatically.

  Important DEM metadata include horizontal CRS, vertical datum, vertical units, horizontal resolution, interpolation method,
  source sensor, acquisition date, void treatment, hydro-conditioning status, accuracy statement, and whether the values
  represent bare earth or the top surface.

  Do not compare two DEMs simply because they have the same cell size. A 1 m LiDAR DEM and a 1 m photogrammetric
  DEM can have very different error characteristics. Cell size describes sampling spacing, not automatically positional or
  vertical accuracy.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  3. DTM — Digital Terrain Model
  DTM is one of the most abused terms in elevation work. In some organizations DTM is effectively a synonym for a bare-earth
  DEM. In USGS specifications, DTM can mean a vector representation containing 3D mass points and breaklines that
  characterize bare-earth terrain.

  The distinction matters because breaklines can preserve terrain structures that a regular grid may smooth or miss. Examples
  include drainage channels, ridges, road edges, embankments, retaining features, and other abrupt changes in slope.

  A DTM workflow may therefore begin with classified ground LiDAR points and add breaklines. The resulting dataset can then
  be converted to a TIN or raster DEM.

  For engineering work, breaklines are especially important because a purely automated raster surface can produce unrealistic
  transitions across roads, drainage structures, or designed earthworks. A well-built DTM can encode known terrain constraints


Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                    Page 8
Page 9 of 60 
  rather than relying entirely on interpolation.

  When receiving a file labeled "DTM," ask whether it is a raster, a TIN, or a vector collection of mass points and breaklines.
  The label alone is insufficient.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  4. DSM — Digital Surface Model
  A Digital Surface Model represents the upper surface detected by the sensor. It can include bare ground, buildings,
  vegetation, towers, vehicles, and other objects above the terrain.

  For LiDAR, a DSM can be generated from appropriate first/highest surface returns or from a surface constructed from
  non-ground points. For photogrammetry, the dense point cloud generally captures visible surfaces rather than the hidden
  ground beneath trees.

  DSM applications include telecommunications line-of-sight analysis, solar potential studies, urban 3D modeling,
  building-height analysis, canopy studies, aviation obstruction analysis, and visibility modeling.

  A DSM is not automatically a "better DEM." It answers a different question. If the question is "How high is the terrain?", use a
  bare-earth model. If the question is "What is the elevation of the top of the tree canopy or building roof?", a DSM may be
  appropriate.

  A useful derivative is Height Above Ground. Subtracting a ground model from a surface model can reveal building and
  vegetation heights, subject to registration and model-quality errors.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  5. DEM vs DTM vs DSM — Precise Comparison
  The simplest practical distinction is:

  DEM: a general digital elevation representation, commonly a raster; depending on the organization, it may mean bare earth.
  DTM: a terrain-focused model; in some specifications it is a bare-earth raster, while in others it is a vector terrain dataset with
  mass points and breaklines. DSM: a surface model that includes above-ground objects such as buildings, vegetation, and
  towers.

  The USGS explicitly documents these terminology differences, so professionals should not pretend there is one universal
  definition.

  For training, use the terms according to the project specification. If a client says "DEM," ask what surface is required. If a
  client says "DTM," ask whether breaklines are required. If a client says "DSM," ask whether buildings and vegetation must be
  retained.

  The worst workflow is to deliver a file based on an acronym without verifying what the recipient expects.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  6. TIN — Triangulated Irregular Network
  A TIN represents a surface using interconnected triangles. Unlike a raster, which samples the surface on a regular grid, a TIN
  can place vertices where information is more important and use breaklines to preserve terrain structure.

  TIN construction commonly uses Delaunay triangulation or related constrained triangulation approaches. The triangle edges
  form a continuous piecewise-planar surface.

Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                     Page 9
Page 10 of 60 
  TINs are useful where terrain has irregularly distributed observations, sharp features, or engineering breaklines. A road
  embankment, channel edge, ridge, or designed grading feature can be represented explicitly.

  TINs also have disadvantages. Very large datasets can contain enormous numbers of triangles. Poorly distributed points can
  create long triangles and unrealistic interpolation. A TIN does not magically improve bad input data; it only connects the
  available observations.

  A professional TIN workflow therefore includes point selection, breakline enforcement, boundary constraints, triangle quality
  inspection, and independent elevation validation.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  7. Raster DEM vs TIN
  Raster and TIN models solve similar problems differently. A raster has predictable storage and straightforward map algebra. It
  is excellent for slope, aspect, hydrology, visibility, raster algebra, machine learning, and large-area analysis.

  A TIN is more adaptive. It can preserve important terrain features with fewer vertices and explicit breaklines. It is often
  valuable in engineering design, grading, corridor work, and situations where irregular observations matter.

  Raster DEM advantages include simple interoperability, fast array operations, straightforward resampling, and predictable cell
  addressing. Disadvantages include resolution dependence and potential smoothing or aliasing.

  TIN advantages include variable point density and explicit linear features. Disadvantages include more complex storage,
  potentially large triangle counts, and more complicated raster-style analysis.

  Many production workflows use both: a DTM/TIN for terrain construction and a raster DEM for analysis and distribution.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  8. Contours — What They Actually Represent
  A contour is a line connecting locations with equal elevation. Contours are derived from an elevation surface; they are not
  independent measurements unless surveyed directly.

  Contour interval determines how much vertical change occurs between adjacent lines. Smaller intervals show more terrain
  detail but can produce dense, visually noisy maps. Larger intervals simplify terrain but can hide local variation.

  Contour generation depends on the underlying surface. A poor DEM creates poor contours. Artifacts such as spikes, pits,
  bridges, vegetation remnants, or interpolation errors can appear as strange contour loops.

  Index contours are usually emphasized at larger intervals to improve map readability. Supplementary contours may be used
  for detailed mapping.

  Contours should not be treated as a substitute for the source DEM. They are a derived visualization and analysis product. For
  numerical modeling, retain the original elevation surface.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  9. Contour Generation from LiDAR
  A typical LiDAR contour workflow begins with classification, especially ground classification. Ground points are used to create
  a DTM, TIN, or DEM. The surface is then contoured.




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                    Page 10
Page 11 of 60 
  Before generating contours, inspect density and gaps. Sparse regions can create interpolation artifacts. Water bodies and
  bridges may require special handling. Road fills and culverts can create incorrect drainage if the surface is not
  hydro-conditioned or hydro-enforced.

  Contour smoothing is tempting but dangerous. Smoothing improves appearance while potentially shifting the actual location
  of the contour. If contours are used for engineering or surveying, the smoothing method and tolerance must be controlled.

  Quality control should compare contours back to the source surface and, where required, to independent survey points.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  10. Bare-Earth Modeling
  Bare-earth modeling attempts to represent the terrain as if vegetation, buildings, vehicles, and other surface objects were
  removed.

  LiDAR is particularly useful because multiple returns can provide ground observations under vegetation, although dense
  canopy can still reduce ground-return density. Photogrammetry is more dependent on visible surfaces and can struggle to
  reconstruct ground beneath dense vegetation.

  The workflow usually involves point-cloud filtering/classification, removal of non-ground points, treatment of bridges and
  water, and interpolation into a terrain surface.

  Bare-earth modeling is foundational for flood modeling, drainage analysis, road design, cut/fill calculations, watershed
  delineation, slope analysis, landslide studies, and topographic mapping.

  The critical failure mode is over-filtering. If legitimate terrain points are removed, the terrain can become artificially smooth.
  Under-filtering produces vegetation or structures in the supposed bare-earth model.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  11. Ground Classification and Terrain Model Quality
  Ground classification is often the single most important upstream operation for a LiDAR-derived terrain model. Algorithms use
  local geometry, slope, point spacing, elevation differences, and neighborhood relationships to decide which points are likely
  ground.

  Algorithms can fail in cliffs, steep terrain, dense forest, tall grass, urban edges, bridges, rock outcrops, construction sites, and
  complex drainage.

  The correct approach is not to search for a universal parameter set. Parameters should reflect point density, terrain slope,
  expected object size, acquisition geometry, and mapping scale.

  After classification, inspect cross-sections. Profiles through roads, ditches, buildings, forest edges, and steep slopes reveal
  problems that are easy to miss in a top-down view.

  Classification QA should also use statistics: ground percentage, density maps, elevation ranges, and tile-to-tile consistency.
  Automated flags can identify tiles that deserve manual review.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  12. Surface Modeling
  Surface modeling converts discrete observations into a continuous mathematical or computational representation. Common
  approaches include TINs, raster interpolation, splines, kriging, natural-neighbor interpolation, and other methods.

Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                      Page 11
Page 12 of 60 
  The interpolation method affects the final surface. A surface generated from dense LiDAR ground points can differ from one
  generated from sparse contours. The model should therefore be selected based on the source observations and intended
  use.

  For engineering, preserving breaklines and known terrain constraints is often more important than applying a sophisticated
  interpolation algorithm.

  For large GIS analysis, a raster is often preferable because terrain calculations operate efficiently on arrays.

  A professional surface model should document source points, filtering, interpolation method, cell size or triangle rules,
  breaklines, boundary conditions, void treatment, and vertical reference.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  13. Terrain Resolution and Scale
  Resolution is frequently misunderstood. A 0.5 m DEM is not automatically more accurate than a 2 m DEM. It simply
  represents the surface at a finer sampling interval.

  The USGS describes DEM resolution as the linear size of a raster cell; features smaller than the cell size cannot be explicitly
  represented. That does not mean every feature larger than the cell size is accurately represented.

  Resolution should be chosen from point density, terrain complexity, source accuracy, intended analysis, and
  storage/performance constraints.

  If point density is low, an extremely fine raster can create empty cells, long interpolations, or false precision. If point density is
  high, an overly coarse raster can erase drainage features, small embankments, and terrain details.

  Choose the resolution that the evidence can support, not the smallest number your software allows.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  14. Vertical Accuracy, RMSE and Checkpoints
  Elevation models should be evaluated against independent checkpoints when accuracy matters. The checkpoints should
  ideally be independent from the data used to create the model.

  Common measures include mean error, median error, standard deviation, RMSEz, percentile errors, and maximum observed
  error. The appropriate statistic depends on the specification.

  A model can have a low overall RMSE while still failing in specific terrain classes. Therefore stratify QA by land cover or
  terrain condition when the project requires it.

  Also distinguish relative accuracy from absolute accuracy. Relative accuracy concerns consistency between neighboring
  observations or strips. Absolute accuracy concerns agreement with an external reference system.

  A strong report states the checkpoint source, vertical datum, sample size, spatial distribution, land-cover distribution,
  statistics, outliers, and acceptance threshold.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  15. Vertical Datums and Geoid Considerations
  Elevation values are meaningless without a reference surface. A LiDAR system may initially produce ellipsoidal heights, while
  engineering and mapping products often require orthometric heights related to a geoid.


Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                       Page 12
Page 13 of 60 
  The relationship is commonly represented as H = h - N, where h is ellipsoid height, N is geoid height, and H is orthometric
  height.

  A terrain model can be internally consistent but shifted vertically if the wrong datum or geoid model is applied.

  Software can also store CRS metadata differently. Some formats preserve coordinate reference information poorly, so a
  workflow must explicitly record the horizontal CRS, vertical datum, units, geoid model, and any transformations.

  Never compare elevation models from different sources until their vertical references have been reconciled.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  16. Hydro-Flattening and Hydro-Enforcement
  Hydrology is one of the places where a generic terrain surface can fail. Natural water surfaces may appear noisy in LiDAR
  because of reflections, sparse returns, or sensor behavior. Roads can also create artificial barriers across drainage channels.

  Hydro-flattening aims to create consistent water-surface representation. Hydro-enforcement goes further by ensuring
  drainage paths and culverts support plausible downhill flow.

  USGS documentation distinguishes hydro-flattened, hydro-enforced, and hydro-conditioned DEMs. Hydro-enforced models
  can cut drainage paths through road fills over culverts, while hydro-conditioned models additionally remove spurious
  depressions to support continuous modeled flow.

  This matters for flood modeling and watershed analysis. A visually attractive DEM can still produce incorrect flow direction if
  drainage structures are not represented correctly.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  17. Terrain Derivatives
  Once a terrain model exists, many derivatives can be calculated: slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, roughness, flow
  direction, flow accumulation, watershed boundaries, drainage networks, visibility, relative elevation, topographic position, and
  terrain profiles.

  Slope measures the rate of elevation change. Aspect describes directional orientation. Hillshade is primarily a visualization
  technique. Curvature describes how slope changes spatially and can help identify ridges, channels, and convex/concave
  terrain.

  Derivative quality depends directly on DEM quality and resolution. Noise becomes slope noise. Small horizontal errors can
  become exaggerated in steep terrain.

  For this reason, do not calculate dozens of derivatives before validating the base terrain model.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  18. Slope Analysis
  Slope can be expressed as a percentage or angle. A 100% slope corresponds to a 45-degree angle.

  Slope is used in road planning, landslide susceptibility, construction suitability, drainage, agriculture, forestry, erosion studies,
  and infrastructure risk.

  Slope calculations are sensitive to cell size. A fine-resolution model may capture small local changes, while a coarser model
  smooths them.


Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                      Page 13
Page 14 of 60 
  For engineering decisions, slope should be interpreted together with terrain roughness, geology, drainage, land cover, and
  survey accuracy. A slope raster alone does not tell you whether a site is constructible.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  19. Aspect and Solar/Terrain Analysis
  Aspect identifies the direction a terrain surface faces. It is useful for solar exposure, vegetation studies, snow persistence,
  microclimate analysis, and landscape planning.

  Flat areas have unstable or undefined aspect values because small elevation errors can produce large directional changes. A
  professional workflow should therefore treat low-slope areas separately.

  Solar modeling can combine DSMs with terrain and building surfaces to estimate shading. In urban environments, DSM
  quality is critical because buildings and trees dominate the visible surface.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  20. Hillshade and Visualization
  Hillshade simulates illumination across a terrain surface. It is excellent for visually interpreting ridges, valleys, drainage,
  terraces, and landforms.

  Hillshade is not an elevation measurement. It is a rendering derived from elevation.

  Multiple illumination directions can reveal different terrain structures. A single hillshade can hide features oriented
  perpendicular to the chosen light source.

  Use hillshade as a QA and visualization layer, not as a replacement for the numeric elevation model.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  21. TIN Construction and Breaklines
  Breaklines are linear features that force the terrain model to honor known changes in elevation behavior. Examples include
  stream banks, road edges, curb lines, retaining walls, ridge lines, and channel bottoms.

  In a constrained TIN, breaklines can control triangle edges and prevent interpolation from cutting across important terrain
  structures.

  Breaklines should be geometrically accurate and correctly attributed. A poorly placed breakline can create larger errors than
  having no breakline at all.

  A good engineering surface often combines mass points with carefully surveyed or extracted breaklines.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  22. Terrain Modeling from Photogrammetry
  Photogrammetric terrain modeling typically begins with overlapping imagery, camera calibration, image matching, a dense
  point cloud, and georeferencing. The dense cloud is then filtered or classified to derive a terrain surface.


Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                        Page 14
Page 15 of 60 
  The main weakness is visibility. Photogrammetry primarily observes surfaces visible to the camera. Dense vegetation can
  prevent reliable ground reconstruction.

  Ground control and RTK/PPK can improve georeferencing but do not automatically solve vegetation occlusion.

  Photogrammetric DEMs are highly useful for open terrain, construction sites, quarries, agriculture, and many UAV mapping
  projects. They should be evaluated for holes, artifacts, moving objects, and vegetation-related errors.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  23. Terrain Modeling from LiDAR
  LiDAR terrain modeling has a major advantage in vegetation because laser pulses can produce multiple returns and some
  can reach the ground. This does not mean LiDAR always sees the ground; dense vegetation, water, steep terrain, and
  acquisition geometry can still cause gaps.

  A LiDAR workflow generally involves strip calibration, noise filtering, ground classification, breakline integration where
  required, and surface generation.

  Point density and scan angle influence the spatial distribution of ground returns. A dense point cloud can still produce sparse
  ground points under heavy canopy.

  LiDAR terrain models are often preferred for high-resolution bare-earth mapping where vegetation penetration is important.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  24. Terrain Modeling from Contours
  Contours can be converted into terrain surfaces, but the result is fundamentally constrained by the contour interval and
  accuracy of the original map.

  Interpolation between contours assumes a terrain behavior that may not be known. Adding artificial points can improve
  numerical stability but does not create real information.

  Contour-derived DEMs are therefore useful for regional terrain modeling when no better source exists, but they should not be
  treated as equivalent to high-resolution LiDAR terrain.

  Metadata should preserve contour interval, source scale, survey date, vertical datum, and known accuracy.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  25. Why Global Mapper Is Useful
  Global Mapper is useful because it bridges several geospatial tasks that are often split across specialist programs. It can work
  with elevation data, LiDAR, raster imagery, vector data, terrain models, contours, and many other geospatial formats in a
  single desktop environment.

  That integration is valuable for practical production. A user can inspect a point cloud, compare it to imagery, generate or
  inspect terrain, calculate elevation statistics, create contours, analyze slopes, export data, and prepare map products without
  constantly switching applications.

  Global Mapper is particularly attractive when the workflow is broader than LiDAR classification. It can serve as a
  terrain-centric GIS workbench.




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                   Page 15
Page 16 of 60 
  It is not a universal replacement for specialized tools. TerraScan/TerraMatch may be better for certain airborne LiDAR
  production and strip-adjustment tasks. PDAL or LAStools may be better for scripted batch processing. CloudCompare may be
  better for certain geometric comparison tasks.

  Global Mapper's value is integration, speed of practical exploration, and the ability to connect terrain processing with wider
  GIS work.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  26. Global Mapper in a LiDAR-to-Terrain Workflow
  A practical workflow can be: import LAS/LAZ -> verify CRS and vertical reference -> inspect density and classification ->
  isolate ground -> create terrain -> inspect hillshade -> generate contours -> calculate slope/aspect -> compare against
  imagery -> export GeoTIFF or other deliverables.

  The operator should not skip the classification inspection. If vegetation or buildings remain in the ground class, the terrain will
  contain false elevations.

  Global Mapper is also useful for overlaying multiple terrain sources. For example, a new LiDAR DEM can be compared
  against an older DEM or surveyed control to identify systematic shifts and local changes.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  27. DEM Difference and Change Detection
  Subtracting one elevation model from another produces an elevation-difference surface. This is useful for construction
  progress, erosion, landslide monitoring, stockpile volume change, flood impacts, quarry excavation, and terrain deformation.

  The two surfaces must be aligned horizontally and vertically. Different resolutions, interpolation methods, vertical datums, and
  acquisition geometries can create apparent change that is not real.

  A strong change-detection workflow includes co-registration, stable-area testing, uncertainty estimation, thresholding, and
  reporting of significant changes rather than treating every pixel difference as meaningful.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  28. Cut/Fill and Volume Analysis
  Volume calculations compare a terrain surface against another surface or a reference plane. They are widely used for
  earthworks, stockpiles, mining, construction, and site grading.

  Accuracy depends on the surfaces, boundaries, breaklines, interpolation, and vertical control.

  A common mistake is to calculate volume from an unvalidated surface. If the terrain contains vegetation or scan noise, the
  resulting volume can be biased.

  Always document the base surface, comparison surface, boundary polygon, units, coordinate system, vertical datum, and
  calculation method.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                    Page 16
Page 17 of 60 
  29. Terrain Profiles and Cross-Sections
  A profile extracts elevation along a line. Profiles are among the simplest and most powerful QA tools because they convert a
  complex surface into a visually interpretable vertical section.

  Profiles are useful for roads, railways, pipelines, drainage channels, riverbanks, embankments, ridges, and construction
  grading.

  For LiDAR QA, draw profiles across difficult boundaries: forest-to-open ground, road-to-ditch, roof-to-ground,
  bridge-to-channel, and steep terrain. Incorrect classification and interpolation often become obvious immediately.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  30. Terrain Analysis for Hydrology
  Terrain is the foundation for many hydrologic analyses. Flow direction and accumulation are commonly derived from a DEM,
  after appropriate conditioning.

  A poor DEM can create artificial sinks, blocked drainage, incorrect watershed boundaries, and unrealistic stream networks.

  Hydro-conditioning should not be applied blindly. Filling every depression can remove real closed basins. Hydrologic
  treatment should match the intended application and data specification.

  For engineering flood studies, terrain modeling should also account for bridges, culverts, levees, channels, and other
  structures that influence flow.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  31. Terrain Analysis for Transportation
  Road and rail planning depend on terrain elevation, slope, curvature, drainage, and earthwork quantities.

  A terrain model can support preliminary alignment studies, longitudinal profiles, cross-sections, cut/fill estimates,
  sight-distance analysis, drainage assessment, and construction monitoring.

  However, a desktop DEM is not automatically a construction-grade survey. Design decisions should use the accuracy level
  appropriate to the project stage and be validated with survey control where required.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  32. Terrain Analysis for Utilities
  Powerlines, pipelines, telecommunications corridors, and roads all interact with terrain.

  A DTM provides ground elevation. A DSM adds vegetation and structures. Combining the two helps identify clearance,
  access, visibility, drainage, and construction constraints.

  For utility corridor work, terrain analysis should be combined with asset geometry and vegetation classification. A terrain-only
  model cannot answer vegetation encroachment questions.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                 Page 17
Page 18 of 60 
  33. Terrain Analysis for Forestry
  Forestry commonly uses a DTM to normalize LiDAR heights. The Canopy Height Model can be approximated as DSM minus
  DTM.

  This enables tree-height estimates, canopy density, gap analysis, biomass-related metrics, and stand characterization.

  The quality of every vegetation metric depends on the terrain model. A 2 m vertical terrain error can become a 2 m error in
  every derived tree height in the affected area.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  34. Terrain Analysis for Urban Areas
  Urban terrain is complicated by buildings, roads, walls, bridges, and engineered surfaces. A bare-earth model must
  distinguish ground from structures while preserving important terrain features.

  DSM and DTM together can support building-height analysis, shadow modeling, drainage, urban heat studies, line-of-sight
  analysis, and 3D city modeling.

  Urban LiDAR often requires more manual QA because objects are geometrically complex and densely packed.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  35. Terrain Analysis for Disaster Assessment
  After floods, landslides, storms, earthquakes, or construction failures, terrain models can quantify changes.

  Before-and-after DEM differencing can reveal erosion, deposition, excavation, collapse, or sediment movement. DSMs can
  reveal changes to buildings and vegetation.

  The key challenge is uncertainty. A 10 cm apparent change is meaningless if the combined vertical uncertainty of the two
  surfaces is 20 cm.

  Disaster analysis should therefore include uncertainty thresholds and stable-ground validation.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  36. Terrain Model File Formats
  Common terrain outputs include GeoTIFF rasters, ASCII grids, XYZ tables, LAS/LAZ point clouds, TIN-related formats, and
  proprietary project formats.

  GeoTIFF is widely useful for raster elevation because it can store georeferencing and numerical cell values. LAS/LAZ is
  appropriate for point-level data. TINs may be stored in application-specific structures or converted to mesh-like formats.

  Format choice should follow downstream use. Keep the authoritative high-resolution source and publish derivatives rather
  than repeatedly converting the only copy.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                   Page 18
Page 19 of 60 
  37. NoData, Voids and Interpolation
  Elevation rasters can contain NoData cells where no valid elevation exists. Interpolating across a small gap may be
  reasonable; interpolating across a large unsurveyed region can manufacture terrain.

  Void handling must be documented. A filled DEM can look complete while containing synthetic values.

  For analysis, preserve a mask showing which cells are measured or interpolated when possible. This is particularly important
  for scientific and engineering work.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  38. Edge Effects and Tile Mosaicking
  Terrain datasets are often tiled. Each tile may be generated independently and later mosaicked.

  If neighboring tiles use inconsistent vertical offsets, classification, interpolation, or edge rules, visible seams can appear.

  Always test tile boundaries. A terrain model can look perfect within each tile and still show discontinuities at the edges.

  Production workflows should include overlap or edge validation and consistent processing parameters across all tiles.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  39. Data Resolution vs Point Density
  Point density describes how many observations exist per unit area. Raster resolution describes the spacing of output cells.
  They are related but not identical.

  A dense point cloud can support a fine raster, but only if the ground observations are also dense and accurate. A high total
  density dominated by vegetation does not imply high ground density.

  When designing a DEM specification, consider ground-point density, not merely total point density.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  40. Terrain Model Generalization
  Generalization reduces detail to make a dataset suitable for a smaller map scale or faster computation.

  Examples include raster resampling, point thinning, contour simplification, TIN decimation, and smoothing.

  Generalization always removes information. The question is whether the removed information is important for the intended
  use.

  Never generalize an authoritative terrain model and then overwrite the original. Keep the full-resolution source.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  41. Terrain Modeling and Machine Learning


Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                        Page 19
Page 20 of 60 
  Terrain models can become inputs to machine-learning systems. Common features include elevation, slope, aspect,
  curvature, roughness, relative elevation, and distance to drainage.

  The danger is that model performance can reflect artifacts in the terrain source rather than real landscape relationships.

  Feature generation should therefore be based on validated terrain and documented resolution. Train/test splits should also
  respect spatial autocorrelation; random pixel splits can produce unrealistically optimistic accuracy.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  42. Terrain Model QA Checklist
  A professional QA checklist should verify: source completeness; point density; ground classification; coordinate reference
  system; vertical datum; geoid model; cell size; interpolation method; breaklines; hydro treatment; NoData areas; edge
  continuity; checkpoint accuracy; slope artifacts; contour artifacts; and metadata.

  Review at least a sample of difficult areas, not only random flat terrain.

  Record software version and processing parameters so the result can be reproduced.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  43. Common Terrain Modeling Mistakes
  Mistake 1: Calling every elevation raster a DTM.

  Mistake 2: Assuming DEM always means the same thing everywhere.

  Mistake 3: Building a DTM from unclassified LiDAR.

  Mistake 4: Choosing raster resolution based only on desired appearance.

  Mistake 5: Filling all depressions without understanding hydrology.

  Mistake 6: Ignoring vertical datum.

  Mistake 7: Generating contours from an unvalidated surface.

  Mistake 8: Treating a DSM as terrain.

  Mistake 9: Using photogrammetric ground data beneath dense canopy without validation.

  Mistake 10: Reporting RMSE without explaining checkpoint distribution and datum.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  44. Professional Workflow Blueprint
  The strongest general workflow is: define specification -> inspect source -> establish CRS and vertical datum ->
  calibrate/clean -> classify ground -> add or verify breaklines -> construct terrain -> validate -> generate derivatives -> produce
  contours -> analyze -> export -> archive.

  Global Mapper can be an efficient hub for many of these steps, especially when LiDAR, raster, vector, terrain, contours, and
  map production need to be handled together. Specialized applications can still be inserted where their algorithms or
  production controls are superior.




Terrain & Elevation Models — Deep-Dive Guide                                                                                   Page 20
Page 21 of 60 
  The goal is not to produce the prettiest terrain model. The goal is to produce a model whose meaning, accuracy, limitations,
  and processing history are known.

  Production checkpoint

  Source → CRS/vertical datum → Surface definition → Resolution/triangulation → QA → Derivatives → Metadata




  Deep-Dive: DEM resolution and scale
  The practical meaning of DEM resolution and scale is best understood by separating measurement from representation.
  Begin with the source observations and ask what physical surface they actually measure. Then identify the filtering,
  classification, interpolation, or transformation required to obtain the intended terrain product. For production work, record the
  coordinate reference system, vertical datum, point density, acquisition method, cell size or triangle rules, interpolation method,
  and quality-control thresholds. The result must be checked visually and numerically. Difficult terrain should be sampled
  deliberately: steep slopes, drainage channels, forest edges, roads, structures, water, and tile boundaries. A terrain product
  that looks smooth may still be wrong, so independent checkpoints and stable-area comparisons should be used when
  accuracy matters. Finally, retain the source and processing lineage so the model can be regenerated rather than becoming an
  undocumented final raster.


  Applied Analysis: vertical datum and geoid
  For vertical datum and geoid, the correct workflow is application-driven. First define the decision the model will support. A
  flood model, engineering grading plan, forestry inventory, solar analysis, or map visualization may require different surface
  characteristics and resolutions. Select the terrain representation accordingly. Then test the model against independent
  observations and known terrain features. Pay special attention to vertical datum, horizontal alignment, resolution, interpolation
  artifacts, and uncertainty. Do not interpret every local difference as a physical feature. Some differences arise from acquisition
  geometry, filtering, interpolation, or registration. A defensible analysis separates real terrain signal from model error.


  QA/QC Module: orthometric vs ellipsoidal height
  Quality control for orthometric vs ellipsoidal height should include metadata inspection, spatial completeness, coordinate
  validation, vertical reference verification, density assessment, surface artifact inspection, and independent validation. Use
  cross-sections and hillshade to find structural problems. Use statistics to quantify error. If the model will support engineering
  or safety decisions, document acceptance thresholds before processing rather than choosing them after seeing the results.
  Preserve logs, software versions, parameters, and source data.
